narrative:
Based on your academic record, the model estimates a 67% chance that you would not pass the bar exam on your first attempt. In other words, if you were admitted, failing the bar would be more likely than passing, and that is why the law school denied your application.

The three strongest factors behind this decision, in order of influence, were your third-year class ranking, your LSAT score, and your first-year class ranking. Your third-year rank was the most important concern: you were in the lowest decile, while accepted students are typically around the sixth decile. Your first-year class rank was nearly as problematic—again, you were at the very bottom, compared with an accepted average near the sixth decile. These two grades-based measures strongly pushed the prediction toward bar exam failure, because they suggest you struggled with the core legal material.

Your LSAT score of 36 was actually a point in your favor, even though it is slightly below the typical admitted student average of 37.18. Among the top factors, your LSAT performance was the only one that pushed toward passing. It simply was not strong enough to overcome the negative signal from your class ranks.

To improve your chances if you reapply, focus on raising your academic record. Take additional rigorous legal coursework, seek strong performance in those courses, and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Address the study habits that may have contributed to your low class ranks. A stronger academic record, combined with your existing LSAT strength, would give the admissions committee more confidence that you can succeed in law school and on the bar exam.
